prize_parts.citation: for foundational contributions to the theory of nominal rigidities and monetary policy: staggered price and wage setting, interest-rate rules, and the micro-founded framework for policy analysis

statement.case_for: I keep B001 first after reading my colleagues' openings. The discovery is a coherent set of ideas, not one result. Nominal rigidities were given tractable form (Calvo's time-dependent pricing, Taylor's staggered contracts). They were then joined to an explicit policy rule (Taylor) and to a welfare-based, micro-founded framework for evaluating policy (Woodford). Central banks use these ideas to reason about policy, so they have shaped practice as well as research. The ideas date from 1980 to the early 2000s. They have been tested through the 2008 crisis, the zero lower bound and the post-2021 inflation, and they remain the reference framework, with the heterogeneous-agent literature extending them. As with the 2020 auction prize, the contribution moved theory into practice. The three names also separate fairly cleanly by role (pricing mechanism, contracts and rule, integrated normative theory). Gali, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum and Smets mostly extended, estimated or quantified the framework, and their contributions are real but come after the originating ideas. My assessment rests on general knowledge and the supplied ballot descriptions, not on independent verification.
statement.case_against: My strongest reservation is attribution. Credit is spread across eight listed names, and any trio leaves out contributors with strong claims, notably Gali and Gertler (and the Christiano-Eichenbaum estimation line). Priority questions also remain around Calvo and Taylor and around figures not on the ballot (Fischer, Phelps). The framework's empirical record is mixed: Phillips-curve performance, the 2008 crisis and the 2021-23 inflation. A committee could reasonably conclude that the discovery is too diffuse for a clean three-person citation and prefer a better-bounded candidate such as B006.

responses.point: Boppart ranks B001 second and proposes Woodford, Gali and Taylor. He treats Calvo as supplying only a pricing device and credits Gali, with Gertler and Clarida, for the analytical and empirical canon.
responses.response: This is the most substantive disagreement on B001. I accept that Gali's work on the New Keynesian Phillips curve is central to the canon, and Gali is my first fallback if the committee wants a more empirical trio. But I treat Calvo's pricing assumption as an originating ingredient. Without it the framework has no tractable aggregate supply block, and the Gali-Gertler-Clarida work builds on it. Clarida is not on the ballot, so a Gali-based trio would also break up a natural group. I keep Calvo and mark Gali as the main attribution uncertainty.

responses.point: Dreber Almenberg ranks B002 first and B001 fifth. She calls B001 the most diffuse candidate and says any three-person selection is contestable. She also notes that the framework's empirical performance has been questioned.
responses.response: I agree on the attribution problem and I list it as my main reservation. I disagree that diffuseness should outweigh B001's significance. The core ideas can be separated by role, and B002 has its own question over Gertler and Gilchrist versus Kiyotaki-Moore. On empirical performance, I read the post-2008 and post-2021 episodes as refining the framework and prompting the heterogeneous-agent extensions, and it has not been replaced. I do accept that Kiyotaki-Moore has a cleaner two-person attribution. That is a real advantage, and it is why B002 stays among my lower-ranked candidates rather than being dismissed.

responses.point: Hassler ranks B002 first. He argues that the Kiyotaki-Moore collateral mechanism is foundational and tractable and shaped post-2008 analysis. He also notes that the 2022 prize partly overlaps in theme.
responses.response: I agree the mechanism is foundational and the pairing is clean. My difficulty is that the 2022 prize addressed banking and financial crises, and the financial-accelerator strand is split between Kiyotaki-Moore and Bernanke-Gertler-Gilchrist. I therefore see less unclaimed ground than in B001, where the core New Keynesian contributions remain unrecognised. I do not think B002 is weak. On breadth of influence over policy practice and on novelty relative to earlier prizes, I still place B001 higher.

responses.point: Teorell ranks B006 first. He argues that political economics treats government as an endogenous actor and that the Persson-Tabellini-Besley trio is coherent and mature. He also flags that the 2024 institutions prize and contested cross-country identification are reservations.
responses.response: I agree with the maturity point and the coherence of the trio, and I rank B006 second myself. Two concerns keep it below B001 for me. The constitutional-effects evidence relies on cross-country variation, where identification is weaker than the theory. The 2024 prize also moved close to this territory. These concerns are about margins and do not undermine the scientific case. If the committee judges B001's attribution too diffuse, B006 is my first alternative.

uncertainties: Whether Gali should replace Calvo, or whether Gertler or Christiano-Eichenbaum should be preferred to any of the three proposed names.
Whether the committee will see the Taylor rule as a scientific contribution or as a policy prescription, and how it will resolve priority questions involving Calvo, Taylor, Fischer and Phelps.
How much weight the post-2021 inflation episode and the heterogeneous-agent critique should carry against the baseline framework.
Whether Gertler's overlap with the 2022 prize and with B002 should affect how the macro slot is allocated.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. I have no documented collaboration with Calvo, Taylor or Woodford. My profile lists SSE affiliation and collaborations in market design, none of which involve the B001 candidates.
